items.title: Iceberg Data Platform
items.text:
An open lakehouse you actually own. Apache Iceberg as the table format, with every other building block open source and replaceable. It runs on a laptop with one command, or on a Kubernetes cluster with Helm.

Getting started with Iceberg takes more than a table format. You need a catalog, object storage, identity, an engine and a place to work. Vendors make that part easy, and that is usually where lock-in starts. This platform shows the other route: Apache Polaris, Keycloak, RustFS, PostgreSQL, marimo and DuckDB, connected through open interfaces (Iceberg REST, S3, OIDC and MCP). You can replace one block without touching the others.

Teams create, own and share their databases. People, notebooks and AI agents all sign in through Keycloak and work with the same grants.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Install Docker with Compose v2 (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows), then run:

# Linux / macOS
curl -fsSL https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

# Windows PowerShell
irm https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex

The installer creates ~/iceberg-data-platform, generates .env, pulls the images and starts the platform. Continue with the installation guide and the first steps.

On a Kubernetes cluster, install the Helm chart instead: see Install on Kubernetes.

items.title: Use it as
items.text:
• A reference architecture. See how catalog, storage, identity and engines fit together with team ownership, data sharing and AI agents on one identity. Every choice and boundary is documented, so you can reuse what fits your own platform.
  • A classroom. The demo-company skill sets up a fictional company for up to 48 participants, with one account each and a sign-in list to hand out. The quick-share skill opens the portals to a room for the session.
  • A personal lab. Learn Iceberg hands-on: create tables in a notebook, follow a query from the catalog to the Parquet files, and try snapshots, branches and Iceberg v3 with no cloud account or trial clock.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
• Administration portal: manage teams, users with a role per team, databases and data shares, and browse every Polaris catalog.
  • User portal: sign in with Keycloak, pick a team and environment, and manage databases, browse catalogs, open notebooks and share data.
  • Catalog details: table schemas, snapshots, branches and tags, partitioning, view SQL and a 100-row preview, plus semantic models with a diagram of their datasets and relationships, all with your own permissions.
  • Data shares: share selected tables, views and semantic models with another team or with an external party, who gets a credential and a DuckDB script, or list them in a data catalog, metadata only.
  • Team notebooks: one shared marimo filespace per team and environment. Each user's execution is isolated and uses that user's own permissions. Ten example notebooks cover PyIceberg, DuckDB, Iceberg v3, two data products whose semantic models live in Polaris (one with DuckDB, one with Polars), and loading API data with dlt.
  • MCP servers: AI agents such as Claude Code sign in through Keycloak to explore data and semantic models, manage databases and data shares, or administer the platform.
  • Extensions: add Conversational BI, a chat over your semantic models, dbt pipelines that agents build and test on your tables, Ingestion (dlt) that loads APIs, databases and files into them, and OpenMetadata, which lists your data products in a data catalog. Each is released on its own.

This is an educational development platform, not an audited production service. Read the security model before deploying it elsewhere.

The presentation walks through Apache Iceberg, the platform and a demo from raw data to answers.

Questions? Start with the FAQ.

items.title: Administration guide
items.text:
The administration portal at http://localhost:3000 (on Kubernetes https://admin.<domain>) manages teams, users, databases and data shares. Sign in through Keycloak with an account that has the iceberg-admin/platform-admin client role. A team role never grants portal administration, including the Administrator role. For the service list, see the first steps; to start and stop the platform, see installation.

You can set up teams, databases and users in three ways: in the portal, through an AI agent over MCP, or with the API. The portal's Getting started page has instructions and examples for each, using this installation's address.

items.title: Teams, databases and users
items.text:
1. Create a team on the Teams page. Renaming a team keeps its stable ID.
  2. Create a database under Databases, or let a team Administrator create one in the user portal. Each database is an Iceberg catalog with its own RustFS bucket, in the Development, Acceptance or Production environment. Names are unique within a team and environment. Team members get access right away, with their role in that team.
  3. Create a user under Users:
  4. Create Keycloak account: creates the account and links it to the platform. Copy the temporary password that is shown once. The user must change it at first sign-in. Email invitations are not configured.
  5. Link existing account: search for the exact Keycloak username. The account keeps its password. Accounts are never linked automatically by matching names.

Select one or more teams and a role per team. Every user needs at least one team. 4. Edit access changes a user's teams and the role in each team. A change to one team leaves the user's other teams untouched. 5. Reset password issues a new temporary password. It only works for accounts that this portal created. 6. Revoke removes the platform identity and its grants but keeps the Keycloak account. Active sessions are refused at their next check, and their notebooks stop within 30 seconds. If setup or revocation stops partway, use Retry setup or Revoke on that row. 7. Rename, move or delete a database under Databases: - A rename or move keeps the catalog ID, bucket and connection settings. After a move, members of the new team get access with their role there. - Deletion is immediate and irreversible. It removes all tables, views, files, the bucket and the database's data shares. If cleanup fails, use Resume deletion. 8. Delete a team after moving or deleting its databases. This is refused if a user would lose their last team.

Role Portal label Access to every database of that team reader Read Read namespaces, tables, views, semantic models and data writer Read & write Also create and write namespaces, tables and views admin Administrator Also manage catalog access, databases and data shares

The portal's user management uses the iceberg-provisioner service account in the iceberg realm. For anything else, use the Keycloak console at http://localhost:8080/admin: sign in as admin and select the iceberg realm. On Kubernetes the console is not published; open it with kubectl -n iceberg port-forward svc/keycloak 8080 and sign in with KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD from the Secret iceberg-platform. You grant portal administration there by assigning the iceberg-admin client role platform-admin. Revoke refuses accounts that have this role.

Lists refresh every 30 seconds while visible. Navigation and filters are kept in the URL.

items.title: Extension service accounts
items.text: When an extension such as Conversational BI is registered, the Teams page lists its service accounts (automation principals): one per team, environment and extension, enabled by a team Administrator in the extension. Revoke stops the extension from acting for that team environment at once. It gets no new tokens, and tokens already issued expire within POLARIS_TOKEN_LIFETIME (one hour by default).

items.title: Data shares
items.text:
Team administrators create data shares in the user portal. The Data shares page lists every share with its database, team, objects, expiry and creator, and you can revoke any of them there. A database that has shares can't be moved until they are revoked.

Recipients outside this machine need addresses they can reach: see deploying beyond localhost. A Kubernetes installation has them already. For a temporary class or demo, the quick-share skill sets this up through Cloudflare quick tunnels.

items.title: Catalog browser
items.text: The Catalog page browses all Polaris catalogs, namespaces, tables, views and semantic models, including catalogs created outside the portal. It shows names only, never data, view SQL, semantic model definitions or credentials.

items.title: Semantic models
items.text:
Polaris 1.8 stores Apache Ossie semantic models beside the tables they describe. The platform enables the beta feature with ENABLE_SEMANTIC_MODELS in compose.yaml. Set POLARIS_SEMANTIC_MODELS=false in .env and restart Polaris to turn it off (on Kubernetes: polaris.semanticModels=false). Polaris then answers 406 and the user portal lists no models.

  • Access: the Reader role of a new database gets SEMANTIC_MODEL_LIST and SEMANTIC_MODEL_READ. Writers and administrators already have CATALOG_MANAGE_CONTENT, which covers creating, replacing and dropping models.
  • Deleting a database removes its semantic models first. Polaris refuses to drop a namespace that still holds one.
  • Where users find them: Catalog in the user portal (the administration portal's Catalog lists their names only), the MCP tools list_semantic_models, describe_semantic_model, query_semantic_model and list_dimension_values (writers also publish_semantic_model and delete_semantic_model), the installation's semantic-model agent skill, and the example notebook pairs 06 and 07 (DuckDB) and 09 and 10 (Polars), which publish and read one.
  • Beta: the Polaris API may change in a later release. Check the release notes before upgrading Polaris.

items.title: Infrastructure
items.text: The Infrastructure page shows service health, per-container resources, PostgreSQL statistics, bucket totals and RustFS disk space. The data comes from the internal monitor collector. The page refreshes every 15 seconds, and buckets are scanned every five minutes. Probe history is kept in memory only. Set MONITOR_PROJECTS to choose which Compose projects are measured; on Kubernetes the collector lists the pods of the platform and notebooks namespaces, with CPU and memory from metrics-server. When you run the portal outside Compose, set MONITOR_URL to the collector's address.

items.title: pgAdmin
items.text: With Compose only (the Kubernetes chart has no pgAdmin): at http://localhost:5050, expand Iceberg Platform → Polaris metadata and enter POSTGRES_PASSWORD from .env. This is Polaris's metadata database. Make all changes through the portal so that grants and bucket policies stay in sync.

items.title: Connect an MCP client
items.text:
The portal serves a Model Context Protocol endpoint at /mcp for platform administrators. Register it in your coding agent. Replace http://localhost:3000 with your PORTAL_ORIGIN if you changed it, or on Kubernetes with https://admin.<domain>.

Agent Register the server Sign in Codex (CLI and IDE extension) ~/.codex/config.toml, see below codex mcp login iceberg-admin GitHub Copilot in VS Code .vscode/mcp.json: {"servers": {"iceberg-admin": {"type": "http", "url": "http://localhost:3000/mcp", "oauth": {"clientId": "iceberg-mcp"}}}} Start the server from mcp.json GitHub Copilot CLI ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json, under mcpServers: "iceberg-admin": {"type": "http", "url": "http://localhost:3000/mcp", "tools": ["*"], "oauthClientId": "iceberg-mcp", "oauthPublicClient": true} On first use. If asked for a client ID, enter iceberg-mcp Claude Code claude mcp add --transport http --client-id iceberg-mcp --callback-port 3010 iceberg-admin http://localhost:3000/mcp On the first tool call

Codex configuration:

[mcp_servers.iceberg-admin]
url = "http://localhost:3000/mcp"
scopes = ["openid", "profile", "offline_access"]

[mcp_servers.iceberg-admin.oauth]
client_id = "iceberg-mcp"

Keep the scopes line. Without it, Codex asks Keycloak for every scope it advertises, and the sign-in fails with invalid_scope (openai/codex#35253).

If GitHub Copilot reports that the server is "blocked by policy", your organization has turned off third-party MCP servers for Copilot. A GitHub organization owner must allow them.

Any other MCP client needs: - the URL (streamable HTTP) - OAuth with the public client ID iceberg-mcp, with no client secret and no dynamic client registration - the scopes openid, profile and offline_access

Keycloak accepts the sign-in callback on any localhost or 127.0.0.1 port. Claude Code pins port 3010, which must equal MCP_CALLBACK_PORT in .env (the chart's mcpCallbackPort on Kubernetes). Sign in with your platform administrator account.

Every call requires the platform-admin role. The tools are the administration API's operations:

  • Read: get_overview, list_teams, list_databases, get_database_connection, browse_catalog, list_users, find_accounts, list_shares, list_automation_principals
  • Change: create_team, update_team, create_database, rename_database, move_database, create_user, link_user, update_user_access, retry_user_setup
  • Destructive: delete_team, delete_database (requires confirm_name), delete_user, revoke_share, revoke_automation_principal

create_user returns the one-time password in the agent's transcript. Treat that transcript as confidential, and reset the password if in doubt. Users connect to the user portal's endpoint in the same way.

items.title: API
items.text:
Interactive documentation is at /docs on the portal (http://localhost:3000/docs with Compose) after sign-in. Try it out uses your session and adds the write headers. From a script, send the iceberg_admin cookie from your browser:

curl -b 'iceberg_admin=<cookie>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'X-Portal-Request: 1' \
  -d '{"name": "marketing"}' http://localhost:3000/api/teams

The table lists the main endpoints; /docs has all of them, including Keycloak account management.

Method Path Action GET / POST / DELETE /api/session Read session / sign in / sign out GET /api/health Public process health GET /api/overview Teams, databases, users and shares GET /api/infrastructure Cached monitoring snapshot GET /api/admin/explorer/databases List all Polaris catalogs GET /api/admin/explorer/contents?database=name&namespace=part List contents; repeat namespace for nested paths GET / POST /api/teams List / create teams PATCH / DELETE /api/teams/{id} Edit / delete a team GET / POST /api/databases List / create databases PATCH / DELETE /api/databases/{id} Move with {"team":"team-id"} / delete including data PATCH /api/databases/{id}/name Rename with {"name":"new-name"} GET /api/databases/{id}/connection Iceberg connection details DELETE /api/shares/{id} Revoke a data share GET /api/automation-principals List extension service accounts DELETE /api/automation-principals/{id} Revoke an extension service account GET / POST /api/users List / create users PATCH / DELETE /api/users/{id} Replace memberships with {"memberships":[{"team":"team-id","role":"writer"}]} / revoke

Mutations require Content-Type: application/json and X-Portal-Request: 1, including a DELETE without a body. Errors return {"error": ...} with status 422 (validation), 404 (not found) or 409 (conflict).

items.title: Operations
items.text:
• Run one portal replica; see deployment boundaries.
  • Creations and moves roll back when Polaris or RustFS fails. Database deletion can always be resumed.
  • Polaris 1.8 does not create the PostgreSQL schema when it bootstraps, so compose.yaml and the Helm chart name it (currentSchema=public in the JDBC URL). A different schema must exist before the first start.
  • List calls return pages when a client sends a pageToken (LIST_PAGINATION_ENABLED). Without a token the answer is complete, as the Iceberg REST specification requires, so DuckDB and PyIceberg see every table.
  • To stop the platform or reset all data, see stop and preserve data, or on Kubernetes uninstall.

items.title: Agent skills
items.text:
The installation folder contains six skills for coding agents in .agents/skills, in the open Agent Skills format, and an AGENTS.md (with a CLAUDE.md pointer) that explains iceberg_connect.py, the MCP servers and semantic models to any agent started there. Start your agent in the installation folder and ask it to use a skill, for example "Set up a demo company for my class".

  • Read .agents/skills by themselves: Codex, GitHub Copilot (VS Code and CLI), Gemini CLI and Cursor.
  • Claude Code only reads .claude/skills. The installer adds a pointer there for each skill, so it finds them too.

The skills that use the platform's MCP server explain how to connect each agent. The same steps are in AI agents and the administration guide.

  • quick-share makes the portals reachable from anywhere for a temporary session, such as a class with demo-company. It starts two free Cloudflare quick tunnels with public trycloudflare.com addresses and trusted certificates, so nobody installs an app or imports a certificate. It is for the Compose installation; the Kubernetes chart has HTTPS hosts of its own.
    • Participants use only the user portal address. It also carries the Iceberg catalog and S3 API, so DuckDB and PyIceberg on their own laptops work too.
    • The other address serves the administration portal and sign-in.
    • With Conversational BI installed, a third address serves the chat, linked from the user portal. The dbt and Ingestion extensions are not shared this way.
    • A gateway keeps the Keycloak administration console, the Polaris management API and the RustFS console off the internet.
    • The addresses are random, public and change whenever the tunnels restart, so end the session with the skill's undo.
  • demo-company sets up a fictional Energy, Webshop or Retail company for a class or training through the administration MCP server. It creates one account for each of up to 48 participants in teams of about 4, each with its own databases, gives the platform administrator read-only access to every team, and ends with a printable page of sign-in slips. Connect the agent to the administration MCP server first; the skill explains how.
  • semantic-model creates or improves a semantic model for tables you can write. It first interviews you about the business questions the model must answer, profiles the data, drafts datasets, joins, metrics and AI instructions, runs every question and metric against the real tables, and publishes to Polaris only after you approve. It signs in through iceberg_connect.py as you.
  • kubernetes-install installs the platform on a Kubernetes cluster with its Helm charts, and upgrades or removes it. It first checks the cluster (ingress controller, cert-manager, storage, and that NetworkPolicies are enforced), asks for the domain, certificates, bundled or managed PostgreSQL and the extensions, installs them after you approve each command, checks every host from the outside and tells you where to sign in. It works only in the namespace you confirm. Start your agent in the installation folder or a checkout of the repository, with kubectl pointing at the cluster.
  • dbt-platform builds, tests and schedules dbt pipelines through the dbt extension's MCP server. It finds the source tables with the user portal's MCP tools, works on a branch, and offers a semantic model for each finished mart. Without the dbt extension it tells you how to add it.
  • ingestion loads data from an API, a database or files through the Ingestion extension's MCP server. It starts from a template, keeps secrets out of the pipeline definition, runs the load and checks the result with the user portal's MCP tools. Without the extension it tells you how to add it.

The skills are updated with the installer. Keep your own changes in a copy under another name.

items.title: AI agents
items.text:
Both portals serve a Model Context Protocol endpoint at /mcp, so an AI agent works with your data with your own permissions. On the first tool call the agent opens Keycloak in your browser; sign in with your own account.

Server Address Keycloak client For User portal http://localhost:3002/mcp iceberg-mcp Databases, catalog, semantic models and data shares, as you. See MCP tools Administration portal http://localhost:3000/mcp iceberg-mcp Teams, users and databases, with the platform-admin role. See the administration guide Conversational BI http://localhost:3007/mcp ext-conversationalbi-mcp Governed questions over semantic models. See Conversational BI dbt pipelines http://localhost:3004/mcp ext-dbt-mcp Building, testing and scheduling pipelines. See dbt pipelines Ingestion (dlt) http://localhost:3008/mcp ext-ingestion-mcp Loading APIs, databases and files. See Ingestion (dlt)

The extension servers exist only when that extension is installed. On Kubernetes the addresses are https://users.<domain>/mcp, https://admin.<domain>/mcp and https://<host>.<domain>/mcp for each extension; see addresses and sign-in. Use them in the commands below instead of the localhost ones.

items.title: Connect the user portal
items.text:
# Claude Code
claude mcp add --transport http --client-id iceberg-mcp --callback-port 3010 iceberg-user http://localhost:3002/mcp

Codex, in ~/.codex/config.toml, then run codex mcp login iceberg-user:

[mcp_servers.iceberg-user]
url = "http://localhost:3002/mcp"
scopes = ["openid", "profile", "offline_access"]

[mcp_servers.iceberg-user.oauth]
client_id = "iceberg-mcp"

GitHub Copilot in VS Code, in .vscode/mcp.json:

{"servers": {"iceberg-user": {"type": "http", "url": "http://localhost:3002/mcp", "oauth": {"clientId": "iceberg-mcp"}}}}

The administration guide also covers GitHub Copilot CLI and other clients.

Keycloak accepts the callback on any localhost or 127.0.0.1 port. Claude Code pins port 3010, which must equal MCP_CALLBACK_PORT in .env. If you change that port, run docker compose run --build --rm keycloak-bootstrap and register the server again. On Kubernetes the port is the chart's mcpCallbackPort, applied by helm upgrade.

items.title: What the agent can do
items.text:
Every team member can browse the catalog, preview rows and answer questions from semantic models. Writers also publish and delete semantic models; team administrators also create, rename and delete databases and manage data shares. Destructive tools require the exact name. An external share's client secret is returned once, so the agent sees it; hand it only to the recipient.

MCP tools describes every tool and why it works the way it does. The agent skills in the installation folder teach an agent common tasks, such as building a semantic model or setting up a class.

• Install on Kubernetes. Run the platform and its extensions on your own Kubernetes cluster with one helm install and your domain. Every portal gets its own HTTPS address. You can use your cloud provider's PostgreSQL and the official Apache Polaris chart. The kubernetes-install agent skill guides you through it. The Docker installation stays as it is. See Install on Kubernetes.
  • Safer by default. Fixes from two security reviews, in the platform, Conversational BI, dbt and Ingestion:
  • Semantic models can no longer be used to sneak SQL into a query.
  • Keycloak locks an account for a while after 10 wrong passwords.
  • Teams can no longer reach another team's storage.
  • When a database moves to another team, the old team's extensions lose access to it.
  • Ingestion run logs hide secrets better.

What is still open is listed in the security review. - Notebooks keep running through a short outage. When Polaris or Keycloak restarts you stay signed in, and notebooks stop only after 90 seconds without them. - OpenRouter in Conversational BI. Set LLM_MODEL=openrouter:<vendor>/<model> and OPENROUTER_API_KEY to reach any model OpenRouter offers. - See who used the Bridge. Its logs show every automation account created or revoked and every token issued. - Fixed: filters that combine conditions with AND or OR on calculated fields give the right answer, MCP accepts semantic models up to 1 MB, and the guides name the correct session cookie and OpenMetadata bot permissions.

• Install OpenMetadata with one command. The OpenMetadata extension has its own installer: it adds the extension to your installation, registers it, asks for your OpenMetadata address and bot token, and starts it. With --demo it also starts a local OpenMetadata to try it out. See OpenMetadata.
  • Gemini 4 Argon in Conversational BI. Set LLM_MODEL=google:gemini-4-argon. Long answers from Google models are no longer cut off.

• List a data product in your data catalog. A data share can now also be Listed in the data catalog: its tables, views, columns, descriptions and semantic models are published without data or a credential, so others can find it and ask you for access. Team administrators switch a listing on or off at any time, with a contact for access requests. See data shares.
  • OpenMetadata, a new extension, publishes listed shares to OpenMetadata 2.0: tables and views with their columns, semantic model metrics with their dimensions, lineage, and a data product per share. Semantic models also become glossary terms, and field labels tags. See OpenMetadata.
  • An AI-ready grid forecast with Polars. Example notebooks 09 and 10 write and read a synthetic medium-voltage load forecast and congestion outlook: Polars generates it lazily, checks it with SQL and writes it with its own Iceberg sink, and the semantic model's metrics run unchanged in Polars and in governed queries. Use polars_storage_options() to read or write Iceberg tables with Polars in your own notebooks.
  • Flights example fields say what they mean. Notebook 06 gives every field of the flights semantic model a description, and a label for the ontology concept it holds, with synonyms and examples where they help. The catalog, AI agents and data catalogs show them.
  • The Extension Bridge contract is now 0.1.1, with the listings capability. Existing extensions keep working.
  • The presentation covers all four extensions, data catalog listings with OpenMetadata, and the current component versions.

• dbt pipelines, the second extension: your AI agent builds, tests and schedules dbt models for your team. Writers work on a branch and build it in development; team administrators merge to main, which acceptance and production build. See dbt pipelines.
  • Follow and edit pipelines in the dbt viewer: every model's status and tests per environment and branch, live builds, lineage, row previews, file editing and schedules. From your terminal, iceberg_dbt.py build, test and show run on the platform and stream the log back.
  • Ingestion (dlt), the third extension: load REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB tables, and CSV, JSONL or Parquet files into your team's databases, on demand or on a schedule. Team administrators set up pipelines and their secrets, which are encrypted and write-only; writers start runs. See Ingestion (dlt).
  • Load data with dlt in a notebook. Example 08 loads paged API data with your own identity and merges on a key, so a rerun adds no duplicates. Use dlt_destination() for your own dlt pipelines.
  • See where a table comes from: the catalog links a table built by dbt or loaded by Ingestion to its pipeline under Produced by. Two more agent skills, dbt-platform and ingestion, come with the installer.
  • Documentation site at https://sanderdw.github.io/iceberg-data-platform/, from installation to extensions. The presentation is at /presentation/.
  • Smaller images (the notebook image goes from 3.3 to 2.1 GB) and updated dependencies. Notebooks get Polars 2; see the Polars 2 upgrade guide for your own notebooks.
Not released; its changes are part of 0.9.0.

• Extensions. Separately released extensions add capabilities through the Extension Bridge. Team administrators enable them per team and environment; they never receive secrets or storage keys. See extensions.
  • Conversational BI, the first extension: chat with your semantic models, including shared ones, and get charts with the SQL and metric definitions behind them. The installer can add it, with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini or Amazon Bedrock. See installation.
  • Any AI agent answers from your semantic models. The MCP tool query_semantic_model builds the SQL from the model's agreed metrics and joins, and reads with your own permissions. See MCP tools.
  • Build semantic models with your coding agent. The semantic-model skill interviews you about the questions the model must answer, tests each one against the real data and publishes after your approval. See agent skills.
  • Where a table comes from: the catalog shows a table's description and, for tables a pipeline produces, the last run, test outcome and upstream tables.

• Polaris 1.8.0 adds semantic models to the Catalog. Explore datasets, fields, metrics and relationships alongside your tables, and use the models with AI agents. describe_semantic_model can also return the stored definition.
  • A semantic model's Diagram tab draws its datasets as tables and its relationships as lines between the join columns. Hover a dataset to follow its relationships, or select it to open the table.
  • Data shares can include semantic models. Selecting a model also selects the tables it reads, and recipients read exactly the shared models, never list or change them. When a share leaves out a table that a shared model reads, the portal and the API name it. Add includeModelTables=true to the API call to add those tables instead.
  • AI agents can manage data shares. New MCP tools list outgoing and received shares, and let team administrators create, edit and revoke shares and replace their secrets. Sharing a semantic model through MCP adds the tables it reads.
  • The flight-data notebooks use semantic models stored in the platform: notebook 06 publishes the flights model, and notebook 07 reads it without local model files.
  • Notebooks get 2 GB of memory by default (NOTEBOOK_MEMORY).
  • Fixed: a second write to a table could fail when connecting with DuckDB from your own computer. Download the updated iceberg_connect.py helper from the portal.

• Participants get going from a single slip. The demo-company skill now also writes printable sign-in slips, one per participant. Each slip holds the user portal address with a QR code, the username and the one-time password.
  • quick-share now uses two addresses instead of three, and your own tools work through them.
  • The user portal address also carries the Iceberg catalog and S3 storage, so DuckDB, PyIceberg and DBeaver work on participants' laptops.
  • The administration address carries sign-in.
  • A gateway keeps the Polaris management API, the RustFS console and the Keycloak administration console off the internet.
  • uv run iceberg_connect.py shell db-… opens the DuckDB CLI with the database attached, on macOS, Linux and Windows. The old duckdb -init <(…) only worked in bash.
  • The helper checks the catalog before DuckDB starts. It names an address it can't reach and tells the user to download it again from the portal.
  • Getting started shows install commands for macOS, Linux and Windows. It also warns when the catalog address only works on the platform's own machine.
  • The administration portal points existing databases at the current S3_ENDPOINT when it starts. A database created before the platform got a public address now works from outside, so S3_ENDPOINT no longer has to be set before databases are created.
  • Updated dependencies, including marimo 0.25.0 and uv 0.12.18. Notebooks still ignore a .env file in the team workspace, so one member's .env never sets variables for the whole team.

• New agent skill quick-share opens the portals to participants anywhere for a class or demo. Free Cloudflare quick tunnels give public HTTPS addresses with trusted certificates, so nobody imports a certificate. It replaces the lan-access skill. See agent skills.
  • The installer ends with what to do next.
  • Fixed: deleting a database could remove the storage bucket of another database when a catalog admin had changed the catalog's bucket property. The portal now only deletes a bucket that its tags assign to that database, and otherwise stops with nothing deleted.

• Connect from your machine: use PyIceberg, DuckDB, the DuckDB CLI or DBeaver with your own account instead of a notebook. Catalog › Connect from your computer shows the snippets for each database; the iceberg_connect.py helper signs you in through the browser.
  • Getting started pages in both portals show the three ways in: the portal, your own tools or scripts, and an AI agent through MCP.
  • MCP works with Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Gemini CLI and other MCP clients, not only Claude Code.
  • Try it out works for writes in the administration API documentation at /docs.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
With Compose, settings live in .env in the installation directory. After a change, restart the platform from that directory:

docker compose up -d --wait
docker compose -f compose.users.yaml up -d --wait users

On Kubernetes the same settings are chart values, set with helm upgrade ... --reset-then-reuse-values --set <value>; the last column names them. See Install on Kubernetes.

Variable Default Purpose Chart value USER_PORT 3002 Host port of the user portal (a host: hosts.users) PORTAL_LAN_IP - Extra binding with compose.users.lan.yaml - MAX_NOTEBOOKS 8 Maximum simultaneous notebook containers notebooks.max NOTEBOOK_MEMORY 2g Memory limit per notebook notebooks.memory USER_QUERY_SLOTS 2 Table previews and governed queries that run at once, for all users together users.queries.slots USER_QUERY_WAIT_SECONDS 15 How long an MCP preview or query waits for a free slot before it reports busy users.queries.waitSeconds POLARIS_SEMANTIC_MODELS true Set to false to turn off semantic models in Polaris polaris.semanticModels POLARIS_TOKEN_LIFETIME 3600 Lifetime in seconds of the catalog tokens of extensions and data-share recipients. Extension runs end 15 minutes before their token expires. A revoked service account or data share keeps its issued tokens up to that long polaris.tokenLifetime MCP_CALLBACK_PORT 3010 OAuth callback port of MCP clients mcpCallbackPort PLATFORM_LISTING_EXTENSIONS - Registered extensions that publish listed data shares to a data catalog, such as openmetadata. scripts.setup --extension … --listing sets it extensions.<id>.listing POLARIS_PUBLIC_URL http://localhost:8181 Catalog address for iceberg_connect.py and external share recipients https://<hosts.catalog>.<baseDomain> S3_ENDPOINT http://localhost:9000 Storage address that Polaris hands out with each table. On restart, the administration portal moves existing databases to it. https://<hosts.s3>.<baseDomain> FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS 127.0.0.1 Address of a reverse proxy, so sign-in limits apply per visitor forwardedAllowIps (*)

Behind a reverse proxy, enable WebSockets and preserve the Host header. See the security model for the isolation and trust boundaries.

Ports and Keycloak addresses are set once, before the first start (on Kubernetes baseDomain and hosts); see Keycloak configuration.

items.title: Connect from your computer
items.text:
Use your own Python, DuckDB CLI or DBeaver instead of a notebook. You sign in as yourself, so your team role decides what you can read and write.

In Catalog, select a database and open Connect from your computer:

  1. Download iceberg_connect.py. The portal fills in its Keycloak and catalog addresses. It holds no secret. The installer also puts a copy with the default local addresses next to .env.
  2. Run uv run iceberg_connect.py login, then approve the code in your browser. The refresh token is stored in ~/.config/iceberg-platform with owner-only permissions.
  3. Copy the snippet for your tool. db-… is the database's catalog name.
Tool How Python from iceberg_connect import catalog, duckdb_connection. catalog("db-…") returns a PyIceberg catalog that renews its token itself. duckdb_connection("db-…") returns DuckDB with the database attached as lakehouse. DuckDB CLI uv run iceberg_connect.py shell db-… opens the DuckDB CLI with the database attached, on macOS, Linux and Windows. It needs duckdb on your PATH. DBeaver Create a DuckDB connection. Run uv run iceberg_connect.py duckdb db-… and add each printed line under Connection settings › Initialization › Bootstrap queries.

Sessions run in UTC, so dates cast from timestamps are the same on every computer; SET TimeZone = '…' changes that for one session. DuckDB attaches read-only. Add --write to write with your own permissions. DuckDB keeps the token it started with, and that token lasts one hour. After that, run the command again (or replace the CREATE SECRET line in DBeaver). uv run iceberg_connect.py logout revokes the sign-in.

The helper turns off DuckDB's metadata-log lookup (SET iceberg_use_metadata_log = false). With the lookup on, a catalog clock that runs ahead of your computer makes the next write to a table fail with "Metadata-log exists but none of the entries were valid". Keep the platform host's clock in sync with NTP anyway.

With Compose, Keycloak, Polaris and RustFS listen on 127.0.0.1, so out of the box this works only on the machine that runs the platform. On Kubernetes the catalog and S3 have public HTTPS hosts, so it works from any computer; download the helper from the portal. The quick-share skill makes it work from anywhere: it publishes the catalog and S3 API on the user portal's address. The Getting started guide warns when the catalog address only works on the platform's own machine. The helper names the address it could not reach and tells the user to download it again.

items.title: Conversational BI
items.text:
Ask questions about your data in a chat. Answers come from governed queries on Apache Ossie semantic models: your teams' own models, and the models that other teams share with your team through data shares. The model owner decides what a metric means, how datasets join and which fields exist; the agent only picks names. Every answer shows the query it ran, the join path and the metric definitions, and charts load their numbers from the result, never from the LLM.

Chat http://localhost:3007 LLM Google Gemini, Anthropic, OpenAI or Amazon Bedrock, set with LLM_MODEL API http://localhost:3007/api/v1 MCP http://localhost:3007/mcp (Keycloak sign-in through the ext-conversationalbi-mcp client)

items.title: Install
items.text:
The installer asks whether to add Conversational BI, then which model to use and its key. At the prompt the key is never echoed and stays out of your shell history. To install without questions, pass the model and its key in the environment:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | \
  LLM_MODEL=anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... sh

$env:LLM_MODEL = 'anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5'; $env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = 'sk-ant-...'
irm https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex

ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS=conversationalbi adds it without a model, and ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS=none skips the question. Allocate 8 GiB of Docker memory with it. Rerunning the installer keeps Conversational BI and llm.env. Pass LLM_MODEL and its key again to replace them.

A team administrator enables Conversational BI once per environment: the Enable button in the chat's sidebar, or enable_environment over MCP. That creates the team's read-only service account for that environment, which also reads the data shares the team received there.

On Kubernetes, install its chart next to the platform's; see Install on Kubernetes.

items.title: Connect an AI agent
items.text:
claude mcp add --transport http --client-id ext-conversationalbi-mcp --callback-port 3010 \
  iceberg-conversationalbi http://localhost:3007/mcp

Other agents are set up as for the user portal, with this address and client ID.

items.title: What it can read
items.text:
Model You can ask about it when In a database of one of your teams you are a member of that team, in any role Shared with one of your teams one of your teams received the model and every table it reads, and enabled Conversational BI for that environment; that team's service account reads it

Everything is re-checked on every question and when a chart loads its rows: a revoked share, a table removed from it, an expired share or a removed membership ends access within 30 seconds. Data is read with read-only tokens of the team's service account. Conversational BI never writes to the platform.

items.title: Governed queries
items.text:
The query tool (and POST /api/v1/queries) takes names, not SQL:

{"metrics": ["on_time_arrival_pct"],
 "dimensions": [{"field": "FLIGHT.date", "grain": "week"},
                {"field": "AIRPORT.code", "via": ["route_departure_airport"]}],
 "filters": [{"field": "FLIGHT.date", "op": "between", "value": ["2026-01-01", "2026-01-14"]}],
 "limit": 500}
  • A metric belongs to the dataset its SQL reads (its home). Metrics of different homes go in separate queries.
  • Joins follow relationships from the home, in their direction, and only onto the target's whole primary key. They can never multiply rows: a dimension that would (such as RUNWAY.length on flight metrics) is refused with fan_out.
  • When a dataset is reachable in several ways, the shortest unique path wins; otherwise the query is refused with ambiguous_join and the options, and via picks one.
  • Metric and field SQL from the model passes an allowlist of scalar and aggregate expressions: no queries, table functions, file readers or unknown functions. Values are always parameters.
  • The worker binds exactly the tables it needs with iceberg_scan over the metadata Polaris returned, then disables local files and locks its configuration. It runs with a scrubbed environment, a 30-second limit and memory limits.

Every result also carries:

  • recommended: the component that shows it best, decided from its columns rather than by the LLM. One metric without dimensions is a KPI, a time dimension a line, categories are bars (sideways for many or long names), and two category dimensions split the bars into series, stacked only when the metric adds up (a SUM or COUNT, never an average). Anything wider is a table. The agent follows it unless you ask for another view.
  • dataAsOf: when the metrics' dataset was last committed, from the Iceberg snapshot the query read. Query cards and charts show it as data as of.

items.title: What goes to the LLM
items.text: The LLM provider receives the conversation, the agent's instructions, the selected model's names, descriptions and owner guidance, the compiled SQL, the metric definitions, and at most 20 rows of each result (BI_LLM_ROWS, capped at 8 KB). BI_LLM_ROWS=0 sends no rows: the agent still charts results, because charts and tables load their rows from the gateway. It never receives tokens, credentials or rows beyond that sample. The owner's guidance is passed as quoted data, never as instructions, and tools can only read what the person could read anyway.

items.title: Change the model
items.text:
The model and key are in conversationalbi/llm.env in the installation directory, readable only by you and given only to the chat's gateway container. LLM_MODEL is a Pydantic AI model string; its provider needs:

Provider LLM_MODEL Variables Google Gemini google:gemini-3.8-flash (the default) GOOGLE_API_KEY Anthropic anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5 ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OpenAI openai:gpt-5.5, openai-chat:… OPENAI_API_KEY; OPENAI_BASE_URL for a compatible endpoint Amazon Bedrock bedrock:global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5, bedrock-mantle:… AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK and AWS_REGION Claude on Bedrock, Anthropic client anthropic-bedrock:global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5 as Bedrock OpenRouter openrouter:anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5, with any model name from openrouter.ai/models OPENROUTER_API_KEY

To keep data on your own hardware, point OPENAI_BASE_URL at a local OpenAI-compatible server. After a change, restart the gateway from the installation directory:

docker compose -f conversationalbi/compose.yaml up -d --wait

On Kubernetes the model and key are in the Secret the chart's llm.existingSecret names (or the chart's own llm.model and llm.env). Replace the Secret with the new LLM_MODEL and key, then restart the gateway with kubectl -n iceberg rollout restart deploy/cbi-gateway. The row limits are query.llmRows and query.maxRows there; see add extensions.

A model that cannot start (unknown, or without its key) does not stop the extension: /api/health reports it under llm, the chat answers with what is missing, and the API and MCP server keep working.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
Conversations live in the runtime's memory and end when it restarts. Results are kept for 30 minutes. One query reads at most 5,000 rows; BI_MAX_ROWS can lower that.

How it is built: Conversational BI internals.

items.title: Data shares
items.text:
Data shares in the user portal lists the shares of the active team's databases, plus the shares that other teams have shared with you. Only Administrators can manage shares.

Choose New data share under a database, pick the tables, views and semantic models, and optionally set an expiry. Then choose the recipient:

  • Another team: its current and future members get read-only access with their own accounts. The database appears in their Catalog and Notebooks, even if they own no databases.
  • Externally: the client ID and secret are shown once. Copy DuckDB snippet copies a runnable script. Send both over a secure channel. The recipient saves the script as read_share_duckdb.py and runs uv run read_share_duckdb.py.
  • Listed in the data catalog: the share's metadata is published to your organization's data catalog, so others can find the data product and ask you for access. This choice appears only when a data catalog extension, such as OpenMetadata, is installed. Add a contact for access requests, such as a team mailbox.

You can combine destinations. A listing on its own grants no access and has no credential.

The recipient can read only the selected objects and can't list anything. A view shares only its definition, so you must add every table it reads, and the recipient can read those tables in full. Selecting a semantic model selects the tables its datasets read; if you remove one, the form warns that the recipient can't query the model without it, and saving names every table that is still missing. External recipients load a shared model with a GET on the address shown with the credential. Edit changes the selection, expiry or listing, New secret replaces the secret, and Revoke ends access immediately. To change the team or external recipient, revoke the share and create a new one.

items.title: What a listing publishes
items.text:
A listing gives the data catalog extension the share's name, description, contact, owning team and database, and for each selected object:

  • Tables: name, description, columns with their types and descriptions, partition fields, row count, last update, and the pipeline that produced it with its upstream tables, as far as they are listed too.
  • Views: name, description and columns. Not the view's SQL.
  • Semantic models: datasets, fields, relationships and metrics with their expressions, descriptions and AI context, and the labels of fields.

It never gives data, view SQL, storage locations, snapshots or credentials. The extension decides what its catalog shows; see OpenMetadata. A semantic model's expressions and dataset sources can name tables that aren't listed, so check a model before you list it. Unlisting a share, revoking it or letting it expire removes it from the catalog. See the resource model for the details.

items.title: dbt pipelines
items.text:
dbt v2 pipelines for your teams' tables. The extension is API and MCP first: AI agents create projects, commit models, compile, build, test and schedule, and people watch the pipelines in a viewer, where writers can also edit a model on a branch.

Engine dbt v2 OSS with its built-in DuckDB adapter and Iceberg REST catalogs Viewer http://localhost:3004 (pipelines, runs, schedules, docs), linked from the user portal as Pipelines API http://localhost:3004/api/v1 MCP http://localhost:3004/mcp (Keycloak sign-in through the ext-dbt-mcp client)

items.title: Install
items.text:
The installer asks whether to add dbt. To install without questions:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS=dbt sh

$env:ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS = 'dbt'
irm https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex

Each build runs in its own container, with no internet and a read-only file system, from the runner image the installer pulls. The extension's launcher starts these containers through the Docker socket; it accepts no image, flag or mount from a request. On Kubernetes each build is a Job in the namespace <namespace>-dbt-runs instead, with the same limits. Rerunning the installer keeps the extension, its projects and their runs.

A team administrator enables dbt once per environment, through an agent (enable_environment), under Settings in the viewer, or with POST /api/v1/teams/{team}/environments/development.

On Kubernetes, install its chart next to the platform's; see Install on Kubernetes.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
• Projects belong to a team and are Git repositories kept by the extension. A new project is empty apart from dbt_project.yml, a README and the namespace macro. main is protected: writers commit to branches, and team administrators merge.
  • The viewer shows each pipeline per environment and branch (main unless you pick another), follows running builds live, filters and focuses the graph (+name+), previews a model's rows and builds a node with its upstream or downstream. Files edits any project file on a branch, Schedules manages schedules and Settings enables environments and deletes branches. Writers create projects there. Team administrators delete them under Settings: the project, its history and the dbt properties on its tables go, the tables stay. Writers can edit a node's file from its panel, save it to a branch and build that branch in development. Team administrators can merge it to main.
  • Runs execute as the team's service account for one environment, with a short-lived catalog token: write for build, run and seed, read for everything else. Two builds of the same project and environment never overlap.
  • Promotion. Development builds any branch. Acceptance and production build only revisions that were the head of main: a merge always adds a merge commit, so a commit from inside a merged branch never reaches them. Their schedules need a team administrator.
  • Pipelines are drawn from dbt's information schema, with each node's latest status and test results. After a build, each table gets the platform's producer, lineage and quality properties and its column docs, so the catalog shows where it comes from under Produced by.
Role in the team Can reader View projects, files, runs, schedules and pipelines; compile, preview and test writer Also create projects and branches, commit to branches, build in development, schedule development admin Also merge to main, enable environments, schedule acceptance and production

items.title: Connect an AI agent
items.text:
Register both the user portal MCP and the dbt MCP. The agent uses the user portal tools to find the team's databases and tables, and the dbt tools to build and manage pipelines.

claude mcp add --transport http --client-id iceberg-mcp --callback-port 3010 iceberg-user http://localhost:3002/mcp
claude mcp add --transport http --client-id ext-dbt-mcp --callback-port 3010 iceberg-dbt http://localhost:3004/mcp

For GitHub Copilot in VS Code, add both servers to .vscode/mcp.json:

{
  "servers": {
    "iceberg-user": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:3002/mcp",
      "oauth": { "clientId": "iceberg-mcp" }
    },
    "iceberg-dbt": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:3004/mcp",
      "oauth": { "clientId": "ext-dbt-mcp" }
    }
  }
}

On first use, each server opens its Keycloak sign-in flow. Both act with the signed-in user's permissions. The dbt-platform agent skill in the installation folder teaches an agent the platform's conventions.

items.title: Use dbt from your terminal
items.text:
iceberg_dbt.py gives you dbt's commands in your own terminal while dbt runs on the platform, as the team's service account. Nothing runs on your computer and it needs no warehouse credentials. Download it from the viewer (Projects › From your terminal, or /iceberg_dbt.py): that copy holds this installation's addresses. It needs uv.

uv run iceberg_dbt.py login                    # sign in once in your browser
uv run iceberg_dbt.py projects
uv run iceberg_dbt.py clone cbs_energiebalans  # the project's files from main
cd cbs_energiebalans
uv run iceberg_dbt.py build --select balans+   # runs main in development; the log streams here
uv run iceberg_dbt.py test
uv run iceberg_dbt.py show --select balans --limit 5
uv run iceberg_dbt.py compile --inline "select count(*) from {{ ref('balans') }}"

Commands run main by default, in development unless you pass --target acceptance or --target production (see promotion). Your local edits are not part of a run until you put them on a branch:

uv run iceberg_dbt.py status                   # what changed since clone or pull
uv run iceberg_dbt.py push --branch add-orders -m "Add orders"
uv run iceberg_dbt.py build --ref add-orders   # build the branch in development

A team administrator merges the branch into main in the viewer or with merge_to_main. Pass revision (the branch head you reviewed with diff) so the merge is refused if the branch moved since.

The dbt MCP server can run these commands for an AI agent. Make the script executable (chmod +x iceberg_dbt.py; it starts itself with uv run) and point DBT_PATH at it:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "dbt": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["dbt-mcp"],
      "env": {
        "DBT_PROJECT_DIR": "/path/to/cbs_energiebalans",
        "DBT_PATH": "/path/to/iceberg_dbt.py"
      }
    }
  }
}

Not available on the platform: show --inline, list, debug, deps and clean.

items.title: Project conventions
items.text:
• schema is the Iceberg namespace. +catalog_name picks the database by its display name, with - as _. A project runs unchanged in every environment.
  • Use +materialized: replace_table (the platform materialization: rows are replaced in one Iceberg transaction, so the table keeps its identity, data shares and docs) or incremental. DuckDB cannot create Iceberg views. table recreates the table on every run.
  • profiles.yml and catalogs.yml are generated for every run. packages.yml is not supported, because runs have no internet.
  • Model and column descriptions become the table comment and column docs; tests become its quality status. Generic tests take their parameters under arguments:, as dbt v2 requires.
  • Development is one shared sandbox per team: every branch builds the same tables, and the newest build wins. The viewer shows main, so build main after a merge to see it there.
  • Semantic models are Apache Ossie documents at semantic_models/<database>/<namespace>/<name>.yml. Every successful build or run publishes them to its environment, next to the tables, and lists them in the run's summary. Descriptions a model leaves out come from the dbt models it reads. The file wins over edits made elsewhere; deleting the file does not delete the model.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• A run ends 15 minutes before its catalog token expires, so after 45 minutes by default. For longer runs, raise the platform's token lifetime in .env, for example POLARIS_TOKEN_LIFETIME=7200 for runs up to 1h45, and restart the platform with docker compose up -d --wait. On Kubernetes, set polaris.tokenLifetime=7200 with helm upgrade. A revoked service account or data share then keeps its issued tokens up to that long.
  • Runs cannot read data shares the team received.
  • At most 4 runs run at once across all teams, and at most 2 of one team (on Kubernetes the chart's runs.maxConcurrent and runs.maxPerTeam). A waiting build holds no slot.
  • The dbt docs site, linked from the viewer, loads DuckDB-WASM from cdn.jsdelivr.net in the browser.

How it is built: dbt internals.

items.title: Extensions
items.text:
The core platform stays small: catalog, storage, identity, portals and notebooks. Larger capabilities live in extensions. Each one has its own version and releases, and works with your data only through the platform's sign-in, catalog and storage, with the same grants as you.

Extension What it adds Conversational BI Ask questions about your own and shared semantic models in a chat. Answers come from governed queries compiled from the model, shown as generative UI: query cards, charts, tables and KPIs. Also an API and MCP server dbt pipelines AI agents build, test and schedule dbt v2 pipelines on your team's tables through an API and MCP server. Each run is an isolated container (a Kubernetes Job on Kubernetes) that writes as the team's service account. A viewer shows each pipeline per environment, and writers edit a model there on a branch. Tables it builds show where they come from under Produced by Ingestion (dlt) Load REST APIs, PostgreSQL and MySQL or MariaDB tables, and CSV, JSONL or Parquet files into your team's databases with declarative dlt pipelines, on demand or on a schedule. Through a page, an API and an MCP server. Each run is an isolated container (a Kubernetes Job on Kubernetes) that writes as the team's service account. Tables it loads show Produced by dlt OpenMetadata Publishes the data shares that team administrators list to OpenMetadata: tables, views, columns and descriptions, semantic model metrics with their dimensions, glossary terms and field labels, lineage, and a data product per share with whom to ask for access. Metadata only, never data

The tables Ingestion loads are ordinary Iceberg tables, so a dbt project declares them as sources.

items.title: Install
items.text:
The installer adds extensions. In a terminal it asks for each one. To install without questions, name them in ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.sh | \
  ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS=conversationalbi,dbt,ingestion sh

$env:ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS = 'conversationalbi,dbt,ingestion'
irm https://github.com/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex

ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS=none skips the questions. Rerunning the installer keeps the extensions you added, with their data. Each extension page describes its own options. The installer doesn't add OpenMetadata: it needs your OpenMetadata server and a bot token, so it has its own installer.

On Kubernetes, extensions have their own Helm charts; see Install on Kubernetes. OpenMetadata has no chart yet and runs with Compose only.

items.title: Service accounts
items.text:
An extension acts for a team through a service account (an automation principal) for one environment. Only a team administrator enables it, in the extension. The account can write to the team's databases in that environment, and reads the data shares the team received there. Platform administrators see every service account on the administration portal's Teams page and can revoke it; see the administration guide. The security model has the details.

How extensions connect to the core is described in the Extension Bridge.

items.title: Frequently asked questions
items.text: Short answers, each with a link to the page that has the details.

items.title: Can I run it in production?
items.text: No. This is an educational local development platform. It has not had an independent security audit, only the latest release receives fixes, each portal runs as one replica, and with Compose the user portal mounts the Docker socket. The Kubernetes chart replaces that socket with narrow namespace rights and HTTPS, but the rest still applies. Reuse the architecture and the choices behind it, not the installation itself. See the security model and deploying beyond localhost.

items.title: What do I need?
items.text: Docker with Compose v2 (Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows) and at least 4 GiB of Docker memory, on AMD64 or ARM64. You don't need Python, Node.js or a source checkout. See installation. On a Kubernetes cluster you need Helm, an ingress controller and cert-manager instead; see Install on Kubernetes.

items.title: Where is the first password?
items.text: The installer prints it at the end. It is also PLATFORM_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env in the installation directory. On Kubernetes, read it from the Secret iceberg-platform; see addresses and sign-in. Sign in to the administration portal as platform-admin and choose a new password. See first steps.

items.title: How should I get started?
items.text: Install only the core platform and follow the first steps. You can add extensions later.

items.title: How do I update?
items.text: Run the installer again. It keeps .env and the data volumes. Save your notebook work and read the release notes first. See update or restart. On Kubernetes, run helm upgrade; see update.

items.title: How do I start completely fresh?
items.text: Stop every Compose project with docker compose down --volumes, then remove the team notebook volumes (iceberg-workspaces-work-*), which down never removes. This deletes all data and can't be undone. See stop and preserve data. On Kubernetes, helm uninstall keeps the data; delete the namespaces to remove it (see uninstall).

items.title: Can people in my class use one installation from their own laptops?
items.text: Yes. A Kubernetes installation has public HTTPS addresses already, for a class of any size. With Compose it works with limits: the quick-share skill gives the portals public HTTPS addresses for the session through Cloudflare quick tunnels, but quick tunnels have serious limitations. For anything more than a short session, use a stable Cloudflare Tunnel, or let everyone run their own local installation.

items.title: I'm a team Administrator. Why can't I open the administration portal?
items.text: The administration portal needs the Keycloak role iceberg-admin/platform-admin. Team roles never grant it, including the Administrator role. See the administration guide.

items.title: What can Read, Read & write and Administrator do?
items.text: A role applies to every database of that team. The roles are described under teams, databases and users.

items.title: A user forgot their password.
items.text: A platform administrator uses Reset password on the Users page, which issues a new temporary password. That works only for accounts the portal created. Reset a linked account in the Keycloak console (on Kubernetes through a port-forward; see addresses and sign-in). See the administration guide.

items.title: A package I installed is gone.
items.text: Packages you install with marimo's package installer go to /tmp/packages and disappear when the notebook container stops. Add permanent dependencies to the notebook image. See notebooks.

items.title: Can two people edit the same notebook?
items.text: Teammates share the saved files, but it isn't a collaborative editor. Agree who edits a file. See notebooks.

items.title: My DuckDB session stopped working after an hour.
items.text: The token it started with lasts one hour. From your computer, run the iceberg_connect.py command again. In a notebook, reconnect the DuckDB attachment or call refresh_table_credentials. See connect from your computer and notebooks.

items.title: iceberg_connect.py only works on the platform's machine.
items.text: With Compose, Keycloak, Polaris and RustFS listen on 127.0.0.1. (A Kubernetes installation has public addresses; download the helper from its user portal.) Start the quick-share skill, then download the helper again from the user portal (Catalog › Connect from your computer), so it has the public addresses. See connect from your computer.

items.title: Why are dates and times in UTC?
items.text: Sessions run in UTC, so a date cast from a timestamp is the same on every computer. SET TimeZone = '…' changes it for one session. See connect from your computer.

items.title: What is a semantic model, and when do I need one?
items.text: A semantic model says what the tables in a namespace mean: datasets, fields, relationships and agreed metrics. Polaris stores it next to the tables. Governed queries such as query_semantic_model and Conversational BI need one, so an agent answers from the agreed metrics instead of writing its own SQL. See semantic models.

items.title: Which AI agents work?
items.text: The docs cover Claude Code, Codex and GitHub Copilot in VS Code and the CLI. Any other MCP client works if it supports streamable HTTP and OAuth with the public client ID iceberg-mcp. See AI agents and connect an MCP client.

items.title: Does my data go to an LLM?
items.text: The core platform sends nothing to an LLM (or anything else). A coding agent you connect sees what its tools return. Conversational BI sends the conversation, the compiled SQL and at most 20 rows of each result (BI_LLM_ROWS) to the LLM provider you configure. To keep data on your own hardware, point OPENAI_BASE_URL at a local OpenAI-compatible server. See what goes to the LLM.

items.title: How do I add an extension later?
items.text: Run the installer again and answer yes, or name the extensions in ICEBERG_EXTENSIONS. On Kubernetes, register it in the platform chart and install its chart; see add extensions. It keeps the extensions you already added, with their data. The installer doesn't add OpenMetadata; it has its own installer. See extensions.

items.title: Ingestion refuses my local database.
items.text: Sources on loopback, private or link-local addresses are refused. For a demo against a database on your own computer, set ING_ALLOW_PRIVATE_SOURCES=true in ingestion/.env and restart the extension. The run then reaches your computer as host.docker.internal. On Kubernetes, install the chart with runs.allowPrivateSources=true to reach sources in your own network. See isolation and limits.

items.title: First steps
items.text:
The addresses below are those of the Compose installation. On Kubernetes, use https://admin.<domain> and https://users.<domain>, and read the one-time password from the platform Secret; see addresses and sign-in.

  1. Open the administration portal at http://localhost:3000, sign in as platform-admin and change the temporary password. The installer prints it, and it is PLATFORM_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env; entering the same one again keeps .env as a reference.
  2. Create a team, a database for that team, and a user in that team with the Read & write role. The administration guide explains each step.
  3. Sign out of the administration portal, because signing in to the user portal can fail while you are still signed in there. Open the user portal at http://localhost:3002, sign in as that user with the one-time password, and change it.
  4. Open Notebooks and pick an example from the notebook selector. Start with 01, which creates the data that the later examples read. See notebooks.
