items.title: Keycloak identity and access
items.text: Keycloak handles sign-in for both portals, notebook tokens for Polaris and MCP clients. Polaris handles teams and data permissions. Startup runs keycloak-bootstrap (on Kubernetes a post-install and post-upgrade hook Job), which provisions the iceberg realm, its clients and the platform-admin account. It creates no demo users, teams or databases. To manage accounts, see the administration guide.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
scripts.setup derives PORTAL_ORIGIN, USER_ORIGIN, KEYCLOAK_ORIGIN and OIDC_ISSUER from PORT, USER_PORT and KEYCLOAK_PORT. Set the ports before the first setup. If you change a port later, you must also update the origins and the client redirect and logout URIs in Keycloak, because an existing realm is never re-imported. Issuer and redirect origins must match exactly, so use localhost.

Keycloak access beyond localhost needs HTTPS and matching issuer and redirect URLs; see deploying beyond localhost. For a class or demo, the quick-share skill sets this up.

On Kubernetes, the chart derives the origins from baseDomain and hosts and imports the realm once, with an init container that runs scripts.setup --realm-json; set them before the first install. Keycloak's administration console and the master realm are never routed: the master realm's front-end address is keycloak.adminOrigin (http://localhost:8080), reached through kubectl port-forward, and because nothing outside the cluster reaches that realm it accepts plain HTTP.

To run a portal directly from source, see contributing.

items.title: Authentication and data access
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant P as Portal
    participant K as Keycloak
    participant C as Polaris
    participant N as User notebook
    B->>P: Sign in
    P->>K: Authorization code with PKCE, state and nonce
    K->>B: Login or existing SSO session
    B->>P: Authorization callback
    P->>K: Code exchange (server side)
    P->>P: Verify signatures, issuer, audiences, nonce and subject
    P->>C: Check explicit user mapping and data token
    P->>B: Opaque HttpOnly session cookie
    P->>N: Start runtime with user access token
    N->>P: Request current token with runtime credential
    opt Access token close to expiry
        P->>K: Refresh token exchange (server side)
        P->>P: Revalidate identity and required roles
    end
    P->>N: Current user access token only
    N->>C: PyIceberg / DuckDB with user bearer token
    C->>N: Authorized metadata and scoped storage credentials
  • Portals use confidential clients with the authorization code flow and PKCE. Tokens are verified against JWKS (RS256). The browser only receives an opaque session cookie. Refresh tokens stay in server memory and never reach browsers or notebooks.
  • Portal administration requires the iceberg-admin client role platform-admin. A role with a similar name in another client doesn't count.
  • Polaris runs in mixed mode. User tokens carry a polaris.principal_name claim naming the linked portal-… principal. Only realm administrators can edit that attribute. The gateway also checks the Keycloak issuer and subject stored on the principal. PRINCIPAL_ROLE:ALL activates only the roles Polaris already granted. Client-secret authentication remains for service identities and data shares.
  • MCP clients such as Codex, GitHub Copilot and Claude Code use the public iceberg-mcp client: PKCE and no secret. Its redirects are http://localhost:<MCP_CALLBACK_PORT>/callback, http://localhost/* and http://127.0.0.1/*. For an http loopback address, Keycloak ignores the port, so agents can use their own callback port and path (RFC 8252) and never a remote host. Both portals accept only tokens with azp = iceberg-mcp on /mcp, so portal tokens are refused there, and they authorize every call. The admin endpoint also needs platform-admin, which comes from the client's roles default scope. Keep token exchange disabled.
  • Tools on the user's computer use the public iceberg-cli client with the device authorization grant: no secret and no redirect. The user approves a code in the browser, and the downloadable iceberg_connect.py helper then calls Polaris and RustFS directly with the user's token. Only Polaris grants apply on that path. The gateway's issuer and subject check doesn't. Access tokens of this client last one hour, so DuckDB and DBeaver sessions don't expire after 15 minutes.

items.title: Deployment boundaries
items.text:
• Access tokens last 15 minutes and renew automatically. Portal sessions last at most eight hours, or less if Keycloak refuses renewal.
  • Notebooks fetch their owner's current token from the gateway. PyIceberg picks it up automatically. A native DuckDB attachment must reconnect to renew it.
  • Signing out ends that portal's session and its notebooks, then signs out of Keycloak. There is no back-channel logout. A session in the other portal, a copied token or vended S3 credentials stay valid until they expire. Disabling an account or removing its admin role doesn't invalidate tokens that were already issued.
  • MCP clients and iceberg_connect.py keep an offline refresh token on the user's machine. It is valid for 30 days of inactivity. Revoke it in Keycloak under the user's offline Sessions, or with uv run iceberg_connect.py logout.
  • Sessions are in memory, so each portal needs a single replica.
  • With Compose, Keycloak runs in start-dev mode with a local database. The Kubernetes chart runs keycloak start on Postgres behind HTTPS. Production still needs backups, MFA, key rotation and audit events.

items.title: Demo fixtures
items.text:
The Keycloak browser tests need optional demo accounts on a development stack:

uv run python -m scripts.setup --demo
docker compose run --build --rm keycloak-bootstrap --demo

On Kubernetes, --set demo=true does the same; the passwords are DEMO_*_PASSWORD in the Secret iceberg-platform.

This creates demo-admin, demo-writer, demo-reader and demo-outsider, with their DEMO_*_PASSWORD credentials in .env. Writers and readers can access demo-demo. demo-private belongs to another team, and the outsider has no platform identity. See Contributing for the tests that use them.

items.title: Kubernetes
items.text:
This page is about building and testing the charts. To install the platform on a cluster, see Install on Kubernetes. Lessons from building it are in dev/kubernetes/LESSONS.md.

The Helm chart in deploy/helm/iceberg-data-platform runs the same images as Compose. Extension charts live in their own folders (extensions/<id>/deploy/helm/iceberg-<id>) and are versioned and released with the extension.

items.title: How the chart maps Compose
items.text: Compose Chart Services on iceberg-platform_default Services with the same names in the release namespace, so http://keycloak:8080 and the Bridge aliases stay valid scripts.setup writes .env The Secret iceberg-platform, generated once with Helm's lookup and kept scripts.setup writes the realm import An init container runs scripts.setup --realm-json in the portal image keycloak start-dev with its own database keycloak start on Postgres (database keycloak) The postgres service The bundled StatefulSet, or postgres.external: no pod, and Polaris, Keycloak and the monitor connect to your server with sslmode (test/test_helm_chart.py renders both) polaris-bootstrap An init container of the Polaris pod, or with polaris.external (the official Apache Polaris chart) a hook Job before the Keycloak bootstrap. The official chart's values are rendered to the ConfigMap iceberg-polaris-values; POLARIS=official sh dev/kubernetes/kind_check.sh tests that path keycloak-bootstrap on every up A post-install and post-upgrade hook Job .env.bridge per extension The Secret iceberg-bridge-<id>, from the extensions value Docker socket in users, monitor and the launchers The backends below

items.title: Backends
items.text:
Every Docker-specific part has a switch whose default is Docker, so Compose behaves as before:

  • Notebooks: NOTEBOOK_BACKEND=docker|kubernetes|none. user_portal/runtime_kubernetes.py starts one pod per session in NOTEBOOK_NAMESPACE. The team's storage is a ReadWriteOnce PVC, so sessions of one team and environment share a node (pod affinity). The portal proxies to the pod IP, which keeps the token endpoint's address check.
  • Monitor: MONITOR_BACKEND=kubernetes lists the pods of MONITOR_NAMESPACES and their metrics.k8s.io usage. It runs next to RustFS, which lets it mount the RustFS volume read-only.
  • dbt and Ingestion launchers: LAUNCHER_BACKEND=kubernetes runs one Job per run in RUNS_NAMESPACE. The runner (runner/remote.py) fetches its staged /work from GET /jobs/{id}/input and returns out/ with PUT /jobs/{id}/output, using a ticket that is valid for one run (see the dbt extension's DECISIONS.md). The launcher is a second container in the portal pod, so both share the artifacts volume. Only that container gets a service account token.

server/kube.py is the small API client the core uses. The extensions have their own copy in launcher/kube.py, because they never import platform code.

items.title: Test on kind
items.text:
The CI job kubernetes does this on every change:

sh dev/kubernetes/tools.sh .local/bin && export PATH="$PWD/.local/bin:$PATH"
kind create cluster
docker build -t local/iceberg-data-platform-portal:dev .
docker build -t local/iceberg-data-platform-users:dev -f user_portal/Dockerfile .
docker build -t local/iceberg-data-platform-notebook:dev -f user_portal/notebook/Dockerfile .
for image in portal users notebook; do kind load docker-image local/iceberg-data-platform-$image:dev; done
helm install iceberg deploy/helm/iceberg-data-platform -n iceberg --create-namespace \
  -f deploy/helm/iceberg-data-platform/values-localhost.yaml \
  --set image.registry=local --set image.tag=dev --set image.pullPolicy=Never --wait --timeout 15m

Port-forward the Services to the Compose ports, write .env with python3 dev/kubernetes/local_env.py iceberg > .env, and the smoke tests run unchanged. dev/kubernetes/notebook_check.py checks what a notebook pod can and cannot reach.

items.title: Test on a cloud cluster
items.text: dev/kubernetes/scaleway.py creates a Scaleway Kapsule cluster with Traefik and cert-manager, pushes the working tree's images to a private registry, installs the chart on <ip>.sslip.io hostnames and checks the routed and refused paths. It reads the API key from scaleway.env (git-ignored). Run scaleway.py down after every session; status shows what is still running. down asks whether to keep the reserved IP, so the next cluster gets the same hostnames; without a terminal it keeps it, and --release-ip releases it without asking.

items.title: OpenMetadata internals
items.text:
The extension lives in extensions/openmetadata. It is one service, om-sync, that uses the platform only through the Extension Bridge capability listings, with its service-account token. It never calls Polaris or storage.

flowchart LR
    Portal[User portal] -->|List a share| Polaris
    Bridge -->|Temporary metadata-only role| Polaris
    Sync[om-sync] -->|GET /bridge/v1/listings| Bridge
    Sync -->|PUT tables, metrics, lineage, data products| OM[OpenMetadata API]
  • Core side. A listed share's principal is never activated. For each listing request the Bridge creates a temporary catalog role with only TABLE_READ_PROPERTIES, VIEW_READ_PROPERTIES and SEMANTIC_MODEL_READ on the listed objects, reads their definitions without storage credentials, and deletes the role. See the resource model.
  • Polling. Every OM_POLL_SECONDS the extension reads the listing summary and fetches listings whose version changed, with If-None-Match. Schema and semantic model edits don't change the summary, so every OM_FULL_SYNC_SECONDS it publishes everything again.
  • Reconcile. Upserts are idempotent PUTs in dependency order: domain, teams, database service, database, schema, tables and views, metrics, lineage, data product and its assets. Then everything under this installation's prefix that is no longer listed is removed. There is no state file, so a restart is one full sync. When a listing can't be read, nothing is removed in that sync.
  • OpenMetadata 2.0.5. Database services are CustomDatabase without a connection, tables have type Iceberg, data product assets are added through /assets/add, and a PUT restores a soft-deleted entity. A bot's PUT never replaces a description that is already set, so changed descriptions follow as a JSON Patch. A foreign key needs its table, so referred tables are published first.
  • ER diagram. Open-source OpenMetadata draws none (Collate does) and renders no Mermaid, so the data product's description carries an SVG drawn from the listed keys, as a Markdown data-URI image, with the relationships as a table. The decisions list every API detail.
  • Tests. Unit tests run against a fake OpenMetadata and a fake Bridge on every pull request. The integration job runs the core from the same commit with a local OpenMetadata 2.0.5 on pushes to main and on demand.

items.title: Install from source
items.text:
You need a running platform (core 0.9.1 or later) and an OpenMetadata 2.0 server.

  1. From the platform directory, register the extension as a listing extension and recreate the platform services:
uv run python -m scripts.setup --extension openmetadata --origin http://localhost:3011 \
  --handshake extensions/openmetadata/.env.bridge --listing
docker compose up -d --wait && docker compose -f compose.users.yaml up -d --wait users
  1. In extensions/openmetadata, create .env and set the OpenMetadata address and a bot token:
uv run python -m scripts.setup
  • OM_URL: the OpenMetadata API as the container reaches it, such as https://metadata.example.com/api.

  • OM_JWT_TOKEN: the JWT of an OpenMetadata bot (Settings > Bots, for example ingestion-bot). It needs the permissions listed in the OpenMetadata guide.

  • Start it:

docker compose up -d --build --wait

http://localhost:3011/api/status shows the last sync, counts and the last error code.

items.title: A local OpenMetadata for a demo
items.text:
compose.openmetadata.yaml adds an OpenMetadata 2.0.5 server (with PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch, about 4 GB of memory) to the same project:

uv run python -m scripts.setup --demo
docker compose up -d --wait openmetadata-server
uv run python -m scripts.om_token
docker compose up -d --build --wait

--demo sets COMPOSE_FILE in .env, so docker compose in this folder includes compose.openmetadata.yaml. Remove that line to use your own OpenMetadata again.

Open http://localhost:8585 and sign in as admin@open-metadata.org with password admin.

items.title: Development
items.text:
uv sync && uv run pytest && uv run ruff check . && uv run python -m scripts.release

See AGENTS.md, DECISIONS.md and the changelog.

items.title: Publishing a release
items.text:
The Release workflow publishes three container images (ghcr.io/sanderdw/iceberg-data-platform-{portal,users,notebook}), the Helm chart (oci://ghcr.io/sanderdw/charts/iceberg-data-platform) and the source and installation archives. Local tooling only prepares artifacts.

Channel Published by Release Image tags Installer Stable vX.Y.Z tag on main vX.Y.Z, marked Latest if highest :X.Y.Z, :latest /releases/latest/download/install.sh or /releases/download/vX.Y.Z/install.sh Branch preview Run workflow on the branch Prerelease SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT plus rolling SLUG-preview :SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT /releases/download/SLUG-preview/install.sh

Every installer is pinned to its own release and image tag. Previews never become Latest and never write :latest. A preview also pushes the chart as version X.Y.Z-SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT, with any . or _ in the slug turned into - because chart versions are SemVer. Its images default to the preview's tag: helm install ... --version X.Y.Z-SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT.

items.title: Publish a branch for testers
items.text:
A branch publishes on demand, either through Actions → Release → Run workflow or with gh workflow run Release --ref BRANCH. To publish a branch on every push, add it under on.push.branches in .github/workflows/release.yml.

The workflow runs the full CI suite and builds AMD64 and ARM64 images. Only then does it publish the exact prerelease and update the SLUG-preview installers. A failed run leaves the previous preview in place.

A preview also builds the Conversational BI, dbt and Ingestion (dlt) images from the same commit, tagged :SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT, so its installer can add all three extensions without their own releases. The platform installer doesn't add OpenMetadata, so a core preview doesn't build its image; an OpenMetadata preview publishes its own installer.

SLUG is the branch name in lowercase, with characters other than letters, digits, ., _ and - replaced by -, up to 60 characters. Branch names that start with v plus a digit are rejected. The workflow keeps the five newest builds per branch. Delete the SLUG-preview release after merging.

To build a pinned bundle locally without publishing:

uv run python -m scripts.release --build --install --release-tag BRANCH-123-1 --image-tag BRANCH-123-1 --extension-image-tag BRANCH-123-1

items.title: Publish a stable release
items.text:
1. Update the version in pyproject.toml, package.json, both fields in package-lock.json, uv.lock (uv lock) and the API versions in server/app.py and user_portal/app.py, and version and appVersion in deploy/helm/iceberg-data-platform/Chart.yaml. npm run check:release rejects any mismatch. Update docs/changelog.md, add the release notes in docs/releases/X.Y.Z.md and to nav in zensical.toml and update the version in the install examples, including the chart versions (the platform's and the extensions') in docs/install-kubernetes.md, the release notes and .agents/skills/kubernetes-install/SKILL.md. Record Bridge contract changes in contracts/bridge/CHANGELOG.md and the version in server/bridge.py (see COMPATIBILITY.md); the Bridge has no release of its own.
  2. Run the checks and the dependency audits:
uv export --locked --all-groups --no-hashes --no-emit-project --format requirements-txt -o /tmp/iceberg-requirements.txt
uvx pip-audit==2.10.1 -r /tmp/iceberg-requirements.txt --no-deps --disable-pip
npm audit
  1. Merge into main, wait for CI, then release each extension whose version changed. The installation bundle installs the extensions from their own releases, so a stable core release requires, for each one, the tag <id>-v<version> of the version in its pyproject.toml, unchanged bundled files since that tag, and public images:
  2. Conversational BI: conversationalbi-v<version>, with compose.yaml and scripts/setup.py in extensions/conversationalbi.
  3. dbt: dbt-v<version>, with compose.yaml, scripts/setup.py and skills/ in extensions/dbt.
  4. Ingestion (dlt): ingestion-v<version>, with compose.yaml, scripts/setup.py and skills/ in extensions/ingestion.

A branch preview skips this check, because it builds the extension images itself. OpenMetadata isn't in the installation bundle; it has its own installer, so this check doesn't cover it. Release it before the core when its version changed, so the core's release notes can point to it. 4. Tag the core commit on main:

git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "Release X.Y.Z"
git push origin vX.Y.Z

The workflow rejects a tag that doesn't match the project version or isn't on main. It then:

  1. runs the checks and a Gitleaks scan of the source archive
  2. builds the images on native AMD64 and ARM64
  3. packages the Helm chart, pushes it to oci://ghcr.io/sanderdw/charts/iceberg-data-platform and publishes the GitHub release with the archives, the chart and SHA256SUMS. A new chart package starts private on GHCR, like a new image: make it public once and rerun the job
  4. confirms that the latest installer URLs serve the new version

To check a release before merging, run Actions → Release candidate → Run workflow. It runs npm run verify, builds the source archive, scans it with Gitleaks and publishes nothing.

Never move a published tag. Fix the cause and rerun the workflow instead.

To inspect the artifacts locally, run uv run python -m scripts.release --build --install --release-tag vX.Y.Z --image-tag X.Y.Z. This writes a deterministic source archive, an install bundle and checksums to dist/. check:release enforces a source allowlist, matching versions, license notices and valid local Markdown links. It also rejects known local secrets.

items.title: Release an extension
items.text:
Extensions are versioned and released on their own, with tags <id>-vX.Y.Z that never mark the latest release. For Conversational BI:

  1. In extensions/conversationalbi, update the version in pyproject.toml, uv.lock (uv lock), conversationalbi/config.py, web/package.json and runtime/package.json with their lock files, the two image tags in compose.yaml and the API contract (uv run python -m scripts.api_contract), and version and appVersion in deploy/helm/iceberg-conversationalbi/Chart.yaml. Date its CHANGELOG.md section. uv run python -m scripts.release rejects a mismatch.
  2. After the merge into main, tag that commit:
git tag -a conversationalbi-vX.Y.Z -m "Conversational BI X.Y.Z"
git push origin conversationalbi-vX.Y.Z

The Conversational BI release workflow runs its CI, builds ghcr.io/sanderdw/iceberg-conversationalbi and iceberg-conversationalbi-runtime for AMD64 and ARM64, checks that both are public and publishes the release with its source archive and its Helm chart, which it also pushes to oci://ghcr.io/sanderdw/charts/iceberg-conversationalbi. On the first publication, set both packages to Public and rerun the failed job. Then release the core.

To publish Conversational BI from a branch without a release, run Actions → Conversational BI release → Run workflow on that branch, or gh workflow run "Conversational BI release" --ref BRANCH. It tags both images :SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT and publishes a prerelease conversationalbi-SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT with the source archive, never the version tag. It keeps the five newest previews per branch.

The dbt extension works the same way:

  1. In extensions/dbt, update the version in pyproject.toml, uv.lock (uv lock), dbt_portal/config.py, the image tags in compose.yaml (both iceberg-dbt lines, the runner image and the RUNNER_IMAGE default) and the API contract (uv run python -m scripts.api_contract), and version and appVersion in deploy/helm/iceberg-dbt/Chart.yaml. Date its CHANGELOG.md section. uv run python -m scripts.release rejects a mismatch.
  2. After the merge into main, tag that commit:
git tag -a dbt-vX.Y.Z -m "dbt extension X.Y.Z"
git push origin dbt-vX.Y.Z

The dbt extension release workflow runs its CI, builds ghcr.io/sanderdw/iceberg-dbt and iceberg-dbt-runner for AMD64 and ARM64, checks that both are public and publishes the release with its source archive and its Helm chart, which it also pushes to oci://ghcr.io/sanderdw/charts/iceberg-dbt. On the first publication, set both packages to Public and rerun the failed job. Its branch previews are named dbt-SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT.

The Ingestion extension works the same way:

  1. In extensions/ingestion, update the version in pyproject.toml, uv.lock (uv lock), ingestion/config.py, the image tags in compose.yaml (both iceberg-ingestion lines, the runner image and the RUNNER_IMAGE default) and the API contract (uv run python -m scripts.api_contract), and version and appVersion in deploy/helm/iceberg-ingestion/Chart.yaml. Date its CHANGELOG.md section. uv run python -m scripts.release rejects a mismatch.
  2. After the merge into main, tag that commit:
git tag -a ingestion-vX.Y.Z -m "Ingestion (dlt) X.Y.Z"
git push origin ingestion-vX.Y.Z

The Ingestion release workflow runs its CI, builds ghcr.io/sanderdw/iceberg-ingestion and iceberg-ingestion-runner for AMD64 and ARM64, checks that both are public and publishes the release with its source archive and its Helm chart, which it also pushes to oci://ghcr.io/sanderdw/charts/iceberg-ingestion. On the first publication, set both packages to Public and rerun the failed job. Its branch previews are named ingestion-SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT.

The OpenMetadata extension works the same way, with one image and no API contract:

  1. In extensions/openmetadata, update the version in pyproject.toml, uv.lock (uv lock), VERSION in openmetadata_sync/config.py and the image tag in compose.yaml. Date its CHANGELOG.md section, and update the version in the install commands of docs/openmetadata.md and the extension's README. uv run python -m scripts.release rejects a mismatch.
  2. After the merge into main, tag that commit right away, because the published documentation already names the new installer:
git tag -a openmetadata-vX.Y.Z -m "OpenMetadata X.Y.Z"
git push origin openmetadata-vX.Y.Z

The OpenMetadata extension release workflow runs its CI, including the end-to-end test against a local OpenMetadata server, builds ghcr.io/sanderdw/iceberg-openmetadata for AMD64 and ARM64, checks that it is public and publishes the release with its source archive, its installation bundle (iceberg-openmetadata-X.Y.Z-install.tar.gz: compose.yaml on the published image, the demo's compose.openmetadata.yaml, scripts/setup.py and scripts/om_token.py), install.sh and SHA256SUMS. install.sh downloads from its own release, never from releases/latest, which stays the platform's. On the first publication, set the package to Public and rerun the failed job. Its branch previews are named openmetadata-SLUG-RUN_ID-ATTEMPT and carry an installer of their own. To build them locally: uv run --no-project python -m scripts.release --build --install in extensions/openmetadata.

items.title: Package visibility
items.text: On the first publication, open each package in GitHub Packages and set it to Public, including iceberg-conversationalbi, iceberg-conversationalbi-runtime, iceberg-dbt, iceberg-dbt-runner, iceberg-ingestion, iceberg-ingestion-runner and iceberg-openmetadata, and the charts charts/iceberg-data-platform, charts/iceberg-conversationalbi, charts/iceberg-dbt and charts/iceberg-ingestion. The workflow checks for anonymous pull access before publishing a preview. Publishing uses the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN, so no registry secret is needed.

items.title: Resource model
items.text:
Polaris is the single source of truth. Users, teams, databases and data shares are Polaris records, stored in the polaris PostgreSQL database. There is no separate application database. A fresh installation has no teams, users or databases.

Concept Polaris representation Application properties User Principal with a dedicated principal role portal.name, portal.memberships Team Principal role marked portal.kind=team portal.name, portal.description Membership Team IDs and the role per team, recorded on the user principal portal.memberships (JSON: team ID → role) Role assignment Per catalog, the user's principal role gets the catalog role matching their role in the owning team Polaris catalog-role grants Database Internal Iceberg catalog with a dedicated RustFS bucket portal.name, portal.team, portal.environment, portal.description, portal.bucket Data share Principal marked portal.kind=share, with a principal role and a catalog role of the same name portal.database, portal.objects, portal.recipient-team, portal.external, portal.expires-at, … Automation principal Principal svc-<uuid> marked portal.kind=automation, with principal roles svc-<uuid> (catalog role writer) and svc-<uuid>-read (reader) on each database of its team and environment; the share catalog roles of team shares received in that environment on svc-<uuid>-read portal.team, portal.environment, portal.extension, portal.created-by

Managed records carry portal.managed-by=iceberg-portal-v2.

Data Where it lives Users, teams, shares, grants and catalogs PostgreSQL polaris database Iceberg metadata and Parquet data RustFS, one bucket per database Saved notebooks A Docker volume per team and environment; on Kubernetes a PVC in <namespace>-notebooks Sessions and notebook state Process and container memory Service configuration and bootstrap credentials .env; on Kubernetes chart values and the Secret iceberg-platform

items.title: Users
items.text: A user signs in through Keycloak and is linked by exact issuer and subject to a Polaris principal with a stable portal-<uuid> ID. Usernames follow the form validation rules. Application users are not PostgreSQL login roles.

items.title: Teams and roles
items.text:
A team has a stable team-<uuid> ID, a unique name and an optional description. A user belongs to one or more teams and holds one role per team. That role applies to every database the team owns.

Role Catalog role Access reader reader Read metadata, table data and semantic models writer writer Also create and write namespaces, tables and views admin admin Also manage catalog access, the team's databases and data shares

Effective access is the union across all of a user's teams. The active team and environment only select what the portal and notebooks show. Changing memberships or roles, or moving a database, synchronizes the affected grants.

For example, a user who is writer in analytics and reader in operations can write to the databases of analytics and read those of operations. If a database moves from operations to analytics, that user can then write to it.

Portal administration is a separate Keycloak role (iceberg-admin/platform-admin), and no team role grants it.

items.title: Databases
items.text:
A database is an Iceberg catalog, not a PostgreSQL database. It has a stable db-<uuid> catalog ID, a display name, an owning team, an environment (development, acceptance or production) and a dedicated bucket. Display names are unique within a team and environment.

Renaming a database or moving it to another team keeps its catalog ID, bucket and data. Deletion is immediate in every environment. It revokes the database's shares and removes all stored data, and an interrupted deletion can be resumed.

items.title: Data shares
items.text:
A data share gives another team, an external party, or both read access to selected tables, views and semantic models of one database. The team and external destinations are fixed at creation. A share can also be listed: a listing extension then publishes its metadata to a data catalog. A listing grants nothing, so it can be switched at any time, and a share can be listed only. A share has a stable share-<uuid> ID that names three Polaris records: a principal (the external credential), its principal role and a catalog role in the shared database.

  • Grants: the catalog role holds exactly one grant per selected object: TABLE_READ_DATA on a table, VIEW_READ_PROPERTIES on a view, SEMANTIC_MODEL_READ on a semantic model. It holds nothing on namespaces or the catalog, so external clients load objects by their full names. For team shares, the catalog role is granted to each recipient member's principal role, including future members, and removed when a member leaves.
  • Views are not filters. The recipient's engine reads a view's underlying tables, so those tables must be shared too, and the recipient can read them in full. A share needs at least one table.
  • Semantic models need their tables. A shared model is only useful with the tables it reads. The portal and the MCP tools add those tables when you select a model. The API names each missing table in warnings, and includeModelTables=true adds them instead.
  • Limits and drift: a share holds at most 50 objects, and a database at most 20 shares. Grants follow the object itself, not its name, so a renamed object stays shared, while a dropped and recreated one does not. The portal shows the difference, and saving the share again fixes it.
  • Ownership: a share belongs to its database. Every current Administrator of the owning team can manage it. A shared database can't move to another team until its shares are revoked.
  • Listings: a listed share's principal never receives its principal role, as for a team-only share, so its grants open nothing. The Bridge reads the listed objects' definitions for a listing extension with a temporary catalog role (portal-listing-<uuid>) on the platform identity. That role holds only TABLE_READ_PROPERTIES, VIEW_READ_PROPERTIES and SEMANTIC_MODEL_READ on the listed objects, the reads ask for no storage credentials, and the role is deleted after each read and swept when the Bridge starts. A listing counts toward the 20 shares of its database.
  • Secret and expiry: the client secret is shown once and never stored. New secret ends the previous one immediately. Revocation and expiry end issued tokens at once. The user gateway enforces expiry every 30 seconds, and every share listing enforces it too.

items.title: Automation principals
items.text: An automation principal is the service account through which an extension, such as Conversational BI, dbt or Ingestion, acts for one team in one environment. A team Administrator enables it through the extension (the Bridge). There is at most one per team, environment and extension. It follows the team's databases in that environment: creating, moving and deleting a database update its grants like a member's. It is never a user, member or portal login. Deleting the team revokes it, and platform administrators can revoke it on the Teams page. Its secret is never stored; the Bridge resets it when it starts and issues short-lived tokens (POLARIS_TOKEN_LIFETIME, one hour by default) that carry either the writer or the read-only role. Team shares that its team received from a database in the same environment are also granted to its read-only role, never to the writer role, and end with the share.

items.title: Run from source
items.text:
Requires Docker with Compose v2, uv and at least 4 GiB of Docker memory.

uv python install
uv sync --locked --all-groups
uv run python -m scripts.setup      # generates .env with random credentials; never commit it
docker compose up -d --build --wait
docker compose -f compose.users.yaml --profile images build
docker compose -f compose.users.yaml up -d --wait users

Rerun the three Docker commands after source changes. Save your notebook work first: recreating the user portal stops running notebooks.

For changes to the user portal only, run docker compose -f compose.users.yaml up -d --build --wait users. This skips rebuilding the notebook image.

The services and their addresses are listed in the first steps. The platform also serves the Extension Bridge at http://localhost:3005/bridge/v1, which accepts only tokens of registered extensions; see the Extension Bridge.

Each extension is built and started from its own folder; see Conversational BI, dbt and Ingestion.

To run the platform from source on a local Kubernetes cluster instead, see test on kind.
